question.problem:
Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}$ if

$$
{y}^{″}+16y=7{u}_{4}(t)\cdot (t-4)\,,\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=3,
$$

where ${u}_{4}(t)=u(t-4)$ is the unit step function.
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{″}+16y\} & =L\{7{u}_{4}(t)\cdot (t-4)\} \\ L\{{y}^{″}\}+16L\{y\} & =L\{7{u}_{4}(t)\cdot (t-4)\}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L\{{y}^{″}\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of the second derivative and the initial conditions $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(0)=3:$

$$
L\{{y}^{″}\}={s}^{2}Y(s)-sy(0)-{y}^{′}(0)={s}^{2}Y(s)-3
$$

To find the transform of the right-hand side, we note that the term 

$$
7{u}_{4}(t)\cdot (t-4)
$$

is in the form $u(t-a)\cdot f(t)$ where $a=4$ and $f(t)=7(t-4).$

Now, recall that the second shifting theorem (time-shifting property) states

$$
L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t)\}={e}^{-as}\cdot L\{f(t+a)\}.
$$

  

So, by the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{7u(t-4)\cdot (t-4)\} & ={e}^{-4s}\cdot L\{7((t+4)-4)\} \\  & ={e}^{-4s}\cdot L\{7t\} \\  & ={e}^{-4s}\cdot 7\cdot \frac{1!}{{s}^{1+1}} \\  & =\frac{7{e}^{-4s}}{{s}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute these back into our transformed differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{″}\}+16L\{y\} & =L\{7{u}_{4}(t)(t-4)\} \\ {s}^{2}Y(s)-3+16Y(s) & =\frac{7{e}^{-4s}}{{s}^{2}} \\ ({s}^{2}+16)Y(s) & =3+\frac{7{e}^{-4s}}{{s}^{2}} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{3{s}^{2}+7{e}^{-4s}}{{s}^{2}({s}^{2}+16)}\end{aligned}
$$
